The [Nobel Prize in Physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physics "Nobel Prize in Physics") ([Swedish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_language "Swedish language"): _Nobelpriset i fysik_) is awarded annually by the [Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Swedish_Academy_of_Sciences "Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences") to scientists in the various fields of [physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physics "Physics"). It is one of the five [Nobel Prizes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize "Nobel Prize") established by the 1895 [will](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Will_and_testament "Will and testament") of [Alfred Nobel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Nobel "Alfred Nobel") (who died in 1896), awarded for outstanding contributions in physics.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates_in_Physics#cite_note-1) As dictated by Nobel's will, the award is administered by the [Nobel Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Foundation "Nobel Foundation") and awarded by the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates_in_Physics#cite_note-2) The award is presented in [Stockholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm "Stockholm") at an annual ceremony on 10 December, the anniversary of Nobel's death.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates_in_Physics#cite_note-3) Each recipient receives a medal, a diploma and a monetary award prize that has varied throughout the years.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates_in_Physics#cite_note-4)

## Statistics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Nobel_laureates_in_Physics&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Statistics")]

The Nobel Prize in Physics has been awarded to 229 individuals as of 2025.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates_in_Physics#cite_note-5) The first prize in physics was [awarded in 1901](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1901_Nobel_Prize_in_Physics "1901 Nobel Prize in Physics") to [Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_R%C3%B6ntgen "Wilhelm Röntgen"), of Germany, who received 150,782 [SEK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_krona "Swedish krona"). [John Bardeen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bardeen "John Bardeen") is the only laureate to win the prize twice—in 1956 and 1972.

[William Lawrence Bragg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_Bragg "Lawrence Bragg") was the youngest Nobel laureate in physics; he won the prize in 1915 at the age of 25. He was also the youngest laureate for any Nobel prize until 2014 (when [Malala Yousafzai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malala_Yousafzai "Malala Yousafzai") won the Nobel Peace Prize at the age of 17).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates_in_Physics#cite_note-6) The oldest Nobel Prize laureate in physics was [Arthur Ashkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Ashkin "Arthur Ashkin") who was 96 years old when he was awarded the prize in 2018.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates_in_Physics#cite_note-7)

Only five women have won the prize: [Marie Curie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Curie "Marie Curie") (1903), [Maria Goeppert-Mayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Goeppert-Mayer "Maria Goeppert-Mayer") (1963), [Donna Strickland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donna_Strickland "Donna Strickland") (2018), [Andrea Ghez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrea_Ghez "Andrea Ghez") (2020), and [Anne L'Huillier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_L'Huillier "Anne L'Huillier") (2023).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates_in_Physics#cite_note-8) Before L'Huillier, each woman only ever received a quarter share of the prize, although Marie Curie did receive an [unshared Nobel prize in chemistry in 1911](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates_in_Chemistry "List of Nobel laureates in Chemistry"). In 2023, L'Huillier received a one-third share.

There have been six years for which the Nobel Prize in Physics was not awarded (1916, 1931, 1934, 1940–1942). There were also nine years for which the Nobel Prize in Physics was delayed for one year:

*   The 1914 prize awarded to [Max von Laue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_von_Laue "Max von Laue") was announced only in November 1915.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates_in_Physics#cite_note-N1914-9)
*   The Prize was not awarded in 1917, as the Nobel Committee for Physics decided that none of that year's nominations met the necessary criteria, but was awarded to [Charles Glover Barkla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Glover_Barkla "Charles Glover Barkla") in 1918 and counted as the 1917 prize.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates_in_Physics#cite_note-N1917-10)
*   This precedent was followed for the 1918 prize awarded to [Max Planck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Planck "Max Planck") in 1919,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates_in_Physics#cite_note-N1918-11)
*   the 1921 prize awarded to [Albert Einstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Einstein "Albert Einstein") in 1922,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates_in_Physics#cite_note-N1921-12)
*   the 1924 prize awarded to [Manne Siegbahn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manne_Siegbahn "Manne Siegbahn") in 1925,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates_in_Physics#cite_note-N1924-13)

*   the 1928 prize awarded to [Owen Richardson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owen_Richardson "Owen Richardson") in 1929,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates_in_Physics#cite_note-N1928-15)

A 2020 study reported that half of the Nobel Prizes for science awarded between 1995 and 2017 are clustered in few disciplines. [Particle physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Particle_physics "Particle physics") (14%), [atomic physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_physics "Atomic physics") (10.9%), and 3 non-physics disciplines dominate the prize in recent decades, followed by [semiconductor physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductor_physics "Semiconductor physics") and [magnetics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetics "Magnetics").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates_in_Physics#cite_note-18)

**Owen Chamberlain** (July 10, 1920 – February 28, 2006) was an American [physicist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physicist "Physicist") who shared with [Emilio Segrè](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emilio_Segr%C3%A8 "Emilio Segrè") the [Nobel Prize in Physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physics "Nobel Prize in Physics") for the discovery of the [antiproton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antiproton "Antiproton"), a [sub-atomic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sub_atomic_particle "Sub atomic particle")[antiparticle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antiparticle "Antiparticle").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owen_Chamberlain#cite_note-:0-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owen_Chamberlain#cite_note-2)

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Owen_Chamberlain&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/82/Chamberlain-owen.jpg/250px-Chamberlain-owen.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Chamberlain-owen.jpg)

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/78/Chamberlain-babette_c.jpg/250px-Chamberlain-babette_c.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Chamberlain-babette_c.jpg)

Owen and Babette Chamberlain Los Alamos badges

Born in [San Francisco, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco,_California "San Francisco, California"), Chamberlain graduated from [Germantown Friends School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germantown_Friends_School "Germantown Friends School") in Philadelphia in 1937. He studied physics at [Dartmouth College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartmouth_College "Dartmouth College"), where he was a member of Alpha Theta chapter of [Theta Chi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theta_Chi "Theta Chi") fraternity, and at the [University of California, Berkeley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California,_Berkeley "University of California, Berkeley"). He remained in school until the start of [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), and joined the [Manhattan Project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan_Project "Manhattan Project") in 1942, where he worked with Segrè, both at Berkeley and in [Los Alamos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Alamos,_New_Mexico "Los Alamos, New Mexico"), [New Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Mexico "New Mexico"). He married Beatrice Babette Copper (d. 1988) in 1943, with whom he had four children.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owen_Chamberlain#cite_note-3)

In 1946, after the war, Chamberlain continued with his doctoral studies at the [University of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago "University of Chicago") under physicist [Enrico Fermi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enrico_Fermi "Enrico Fermi").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owen_Chamberlain#cite_note-4) Fermi acted as an important guide and mentor for Chamberlain, encouraging him to leave behind [theoretical physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theoretical_physics "Theoretical physics") for [experimental physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experimental_physics "Experimental physics"), for which Chamberlain had a particular aptitude. Chamberlain received his [PhD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PhD "PhD") from the University of Chicago in 1949.

In 1948, having completed his experimental work, Chamberlain returned to Berkeley as a member of its faculty. There he, Segrè, and other physicists investigated proton-proton scattering. In 1955, a series of proton scattering experiments at Berkeley's [Bevatron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bevatron "Bevatron") led to the discovery of the anti-proton, a particle like a proton but negatively charged. Chamberlain's later research work included the [time projection chamber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_projection_chamber "Time projection chamber") (TPC), and work at the [Stanford Linear Accelerator Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_Linear_Accelerator_Center "Stanford Linear Accelerator Center") (SLAC).

Chamberlain was politically active on issues of peace and social justice, and outspoken against the [Vietnam War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_War "Vietnam War"). He was a member of Scientists for Sakharov, Orlov, and Shcharansky, three physicists of the former [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union") imprisoned for their political beliefs. In the 1980s, he helped found the [nuclear freeze](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_freeze "Nuclear freeze") movement. In 2003 he was one of 22 Nobel Laureates who signed the [Humanist Manifesto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humanism_and_Its_Aspirations "Humanism and Its Aspirations").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owen_Chamberlain#cite_note-5)

After the death of his first wife in 1988, Chamberlain married artist June Steingart Greenfield, who died in 1991. His third wife, Senta Pugh-Chamberlain (née Gaiser) was the widow of physicist Howell Pugh.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owen_Chamberlain#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owen_Chamberlain#cite_note-7)

Chamberlain was diagnosed with [Parkinson's disease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parkinson's_disease "Parkinson's disease") in 1985, and retired from teaching in 1989. He died of complications from the disease on February 28, 2006, in Berkeley at the age of 85. He was survived by his third wife, his four children from his first marriage, and two step-daughters from his third marriage.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owen_Chamberlain#cite_note-:0-1)

Chamberlain plays a central role in [Jacob M. Appel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_M._Appel "Jacob M. Appel")'s [Sherwood Anderson Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sherwood_Anderson_Foundation "Sherwood Anderson Foundation")-winning short story, "Measures of Sorrow".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owen_Chamberlain#cite_note-8)
